context_blurb:
Evolution is change in living things over generations, driven chiefly by natural selection, one of the best-tested ideas in science. It can be watched in a flask of bacteria and read in DNA. Its parts are simple: inherited differences, more young than can survive, and chance.

Charles Darwin worked natural selection out by 1838 but left it unpublished until 1858, when Alfred Russel Wallace wrote from the Malay islands with the same idea. Both took their key from Thomas Malthus. Malthus argued that people multiply faster than their food supply, so famine, disease and war must hold their numbers back. In such a struggle, helpful variations tend to survive.

Jean-Baptiste Lamarck held that a body's gains in life pass to its young, an idea genetics later retired. August Weismann docked the tails of white mice for five generations, and all 901 young had full tails. Weismann saw support for his germ plasm idea: traits are carried by egg and sperm, set apart from the body and beyond reach of its wounds.

Wilhelm Johannsen raised beans in pure lines, each from one self-pollinating plant, so all the beans in a line shared their genes. Weights still varied, yet a line's heaviest and lightest beans, sown apart for generations, bred offspring alike in weight. The extra weight came from growing conditions, not genes, such as how well each mother plant was fed. Selection acts only on inherited differences.

To a biologist, evolution is a change across generations in a population's genes: in how common each gene version is. So in a wild herd of sheep, a gene for dark wool growing more common in each crop of lambs is evolution. Selection acts on single animals, but only a population evolves.

Genetic drift is such change by pure chance, strongest in small populations. Hunted for blubber oil to perhaps twenty by the 1890s, northern elephant seals now top 200,000, protected since the 1920s, yet at one DNA stretch they show only two types. Only seals that died before numbers crashed can show what the species once carried, and their DNA, from museum skins and old bones, is more varied. That crash was a bottleneck.

Chance can even spread a harmful gene. A typhoon in 1775 left about twenty people alive on the Pacific atoll of Pingelap. One of the few survivors, the island's ruler, is believed to have carried one copy of a gene for total colour blindness, harmless alone; among so few, chance let it spread until about three islanders in ten carry it. This is the founder effect.

Gene flow is genes moving between populations of a species, with wandering animals or drifting pollen. Migrants carry gene versions both ways, mixing whatever builds up in one population into the other: gene flow keeps them alike and works against their splitting. So species usually split only once a barrier, a sea or a river, cuts it off.

Biologists count two populations as one species while they can interbreed and have fertile young; horses and donkeys mate, but mules are sterile. So when populations long cut apart meet again and their hybrid young cannot have young of their own, they have become separate species. A species is not defined by looks, though people often tell species apart by looks.

DNA gathers small changes every generation, so lines that parted long ago differ more. The chimpanzee's genome, read in 2005, matches ours at close to 98.8 percent of the letters that line up; the human-mouse gap is sixty times wider. Humans and chimpanzees had a recent common ancestor, their lines parting six to seven million years ago, the mouse line about 75 million. Chimpanzees are cousins, not ancestors.

Since 1988 Richard Lenski's lab has kept twelve populations of the bacterium E. coli, from one ancestor, in fresh broth daily, freezing samples that stay alive. Fitness means success at leaving offspring against rivals. To measure it, the lab grows a thawed ancestor and a later population in one flask, marked to tell them apart, to see which multiplies faster. Grown alone, each would stop when the broth's little sugar ran out.

Around generation 31,500, cells in one flask began feeding on citrate, present in the broth from the start. Zachary Blount replayed the flask's history from its frozen samples: only cells from generation 20,000 on ever evolved the trick again. So an earlier genetic change had paved the way: the population's history mattered, not one rare mutation equally likely at any time.
